Question: Two circles of radius \(2\) are centered at \((2,0)\) and at \((0,2).\) What is the area of the intersection of the interiors of the two circles?
Solution:
Method 1: Split the overlap into circular segments

Let the centers be \(O_1=(2,0)\) and \(O_2=(0,2)\). The points \(P=(0,0)\) and \(Q=(2,2)\) are each \(2\) units from both centers, so \(PQ\) is a common chord. At either center, the radii to \(P\) and \(Q\) are perpendicular: one is horizontal and the other vertical. Thus each relevant sector has central angle \(90^\circ\).

Line \(PQ\) is the perpendicular bisector of \(O_1O_2\). On the side containing \(O_2\), points are closer to \(O_2\) than to \(O_1\). Consequently, the portion of the first disk on that side lies inside both disks. Exchanging the centers gives the other half of the overlap. These two pieces meet along the chord, and each is a circular segment formed by removing a right triangle from a quarter-circle sector.

Each sector has area
\[
\frac{90}{360}\pi(2)^2=\pi,
\]
and each removed triangle has perpendicular legs of length \(2\), so its area is
\[
\frac12\cdot2\cdot2=2.
\]
The intersection therefore has area
\[
\boxed{2(\pi-2)},
\]
choice \(\mathrm{D}\). Including or excluding the boundary curves does not change this area.

Method 2: Count the overlap inside a square

Consider the square with vertices \(P=(0,0)\), \(O_1=(2,0)\), \(Q=(2,2)\), and \(O_2=(0,2)\). Its side length is \(2\), so its area is \(4\).

Any point in both disks must have \(0\le x\le2\) and \(0\le y\le2\). Indeed, the disk centered at \((2,0)\) requires \(x\ge0\) and \(y\le2\), while the disk centered at \((0,2)\) requires \(x\le2\) and \(y\ge0\). Thus the entire overlap lies in this square.

Within the square, each disk occupies a quarter circle of radius \(2\), with area \(\pi\). These two quarter disks cover the square: the one centered at \(O_1\) contains triangle \(PO_1Q\), and the one centered at \(O_2\) contains triangle \(PO_2Q\). Those two triangles fill the square.

Adding the quarter-disk areas counts every part of the square once and their overlap one extra time. Hence
\[
\text{overlap area}=\pi+\pi-4
=\boxed{2(\pi-2)},
\]
choice \(\mathrm{D}\). Boundary curves have no effect on the area.
